progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: From b06: barriers (airway mucus and cilia), phagocytes and phagocytosis; dendritic cells carry pieces of a pathogen to a lymph node and show them to T cells; innate is fast and broad, adaptive is specific and takes days. From b07: antigens; each lymphocyte has receptors of one shape, made at random; clonal selection and expansion; plasma cells and antibodies; antibodies block, clump and coat pathogens outside cells; a B cell usually needs a helper T cell's go-ahead (named only). From b01 and b03: viruses are not cells and must enter a host cell to copy themselves; viruses use surface proteins to bind host cells. From Year 11: proteins are made by cells from instructions in their DNA. Not assumed: antigen presentation, display molecules, T cell receptors, helper and cytotoxic T cells, cytokines, apoptosis, NK cells, the terms humoral and cell-mediated.
progression.startsWith: Follow antigen presentation and T cell activation. The video opens: Antibodies are good at grabbing viruses outside cells.
progression.stopsAfter: explaining why antibodies can't reach a virus inside a cell; explaining antigen presentation (every cell displays pieces of the proteins it makes, so an infected cell displays virus pieces; dendritic cells display pieces of what they took up); explaining that a T cell receptor fits only a piece displayed on a cell, checked together with the display molecule, not free virus; explaining T cell selection and cloning in the lymph node and that two main kinds form; describing helper T cells as coordinators that release cytokines (the go-ahead for B cells, signals that make cytotoxic T cells multiply, signals that make macrophages better at destroying what they engulf) and kill nothing; describing cytotoxic T cells travelling to the infection, binding infected cells that display the matching piece, and triggering apoptosis so the virus loses its factory, while healthy cells are left alone; contrasting innate NK cells (no receptor made for one pathogen; respond to stress signals and too few display molecules) with cytotoxic T cells; describing the two arms of adaptive immunity and helper T cells linking them; interpreting a killing experiment and evaluating a claim about helper T cell loss.
progression.nextLesson: why a second infection is often stopped faster (route entry bio-m7-b09).

teaching.task: Antibodies can't reach a virus once it is inside your cells. How do T cells find the infected cells, and what do they do?
teaching.causalExplanation: Causes: why a second, cell-based defence is needed (antibodies can't enter cells; hook, scene 2); how an infected cell can be told apart from outside (it displays virus pieces because it is making virus proteins; scene 3); why T cells don't bind free virus (receptors fit displayed pieces only; scene 4); why only some T cells respond and why it takes days (selection and cloning, as b07; scene 5); how helper T cells matter without killing (cytokines switch on B cells, killers and macrophages; scene 6); how the killer finds the right cell and spares healthy ones (scene 7); why killing your own cell helps (the factory stops; scene 8); how innate and adaptive killers differ (scene 9). Visible case: one airway cell changing in place from healthy to infected to self-destructing. Thinking opportunities: two unseen items. Reading load: at most about three bright text items; scenes 6 (three targets of the helper) and 10 (the full strip) are the densest, so each tag dims as the next lands.
teaching.conversationalApproach: Antibodies grab viruses outside cells, but a virus gets into your own cells and copies itself there, so the question is how T cells find the infected cells and what they do. A virus binds an airway cell and gets in; almost every cell cuts up some of the proteins it is making and displays small pieces on its surface, so an infected cell displays virus pieces. T cells are lymphocytes with receptors of one shape made at random, and unlike B cells they recognise a piece displayed on a cell, not a free antigen. In the lymph node, dendritic cells display the pathogen's pieces and the few fitting T cells are selected and multiply. Helper T cells mainly coordinate, giving B cells the go-ahead and signalling other cells; cytotoxic T cells leave the node, travel in the blood, check the pieces on airway cells and bind an infected one, then release proteins that make holes and switch on the cell's own self-destruct program, apoptosis. NK cells are innate killers that recognise stressed cells without receptors for one antigen. The adaptive response has two arms, antibodies outside cells and T cells for cells already infected, and the memory aid is B cells make antiBodies, T cells Terminate or Tell. Two exam questions follow with brief feedback.
teaching.openingDecision: Antibodies are good at grabbing viruses outside cells. But a virus doesn't stay outside. It gets into your own cells and copies itself there, where antibodies can't reach it. So how does your body find the infected cells among billions of healthy ones? In 1973, in Canberra, Peter Doherty and Rolf Zinkernagel helped answer that, and later shared a Nobel Prize for it. The answer involves T cells.
teaching.understandingCheck: 13a explains a killing experiment with three groups of cells (recognition of displayed pieces and specificity, the route's stop for cytotoxic T cells). 13c evaluates the claim that losing helper T cells weakens only the T cell arm (helper roles across both arms, the route's stop for helper T cells). Each ends "Pause here to answer." with a 10 s countdown; the whole card stays on screen during the countdown and after it. Feedback is brief (about 25 to 30 s): the answer, the key reasons, givens underlined in the question strip as they are used, one crossed-out classic mistake. No givens card.
teaching.curriculumScope: B7-IQ3-01: "investigate and model the innate and adaptive immune systems in the human body (ACSBL119)". This video models the T cell (cell-mediated) part of the adaptive system and joins it to b07's B cell part; scene 9 places NK cells in the innate system beside it. Verb "investigate and model": the response strip, the coded display-and-receptor shape model and the aligned airway cell plates (healthy, infected, self-destructing) are the model; attempt 1 investigates a killing experiment.

design.visualSystem: One infected airway board. Left two-thirds: painted cells, changing in place. The airway lining plate sets the scene; a coded zoom box opens onto one airway cell, shown as an aligned triplet (`m7-airway-cell-v1.png`, `-infected-v1.png`, `-apoptotic-v1.png`, all new) that crossfades at the cue where each change is narrated. Lymphocytes: the existing `m7-t-cell-v1.png` is the helper T cell; a new aligned partner `m7-t-cell-killer-v1.png` (the same lymphocyte with a cluster of dark granules at one side) is the cytotoxic T cell, so the two read as the same kind of cell with different jobs. Helper cells carry a small teal ring and cytotoxic cells an amber ring whenever both appear. In scene 9 only, the NK cell is the same `m7-t-cell-killer-v1.png` plate at the same size with a teal ring and no receptor forks, always with its grey tag "NK cell", so it is never mistaken for a helper T cell (no helper appears in scene 9). Coded display model: on every cell surface, small coded cup shapes (display molecules) each hold one small notched piece: grey pieces for the cell's own proteins, red pieces for virus proteins (matching the red spikes of `m7-virus-particle-v1.png`). T cell receptors are small coded two-pronged forks whose inner notch fits one cup-and-piece pair. A grey tag "model: display molecules, pieces and receptors drawn far larger than real" appears whenever the model is first used in a scene. Right third: the `ResponseStrip` from b06 and b07, first three rungs as grey thumbnails, the fourth rung showing b07's five B cell chips (grey) and, beside them, the new T cell branch of five chips lit one at a time. No people, hands or faces: the body appears only as airway lining, a lymph node, cells and molecules; attempt 1's mice and attempt 2's patient are words only. Coded elements are abstract only: the display model, the response strip, a clone tree (as b07), a vessel channel (two ink lines, as b06) for travel in the blood, arrows, chips and glosses. Scale: airway column cell about 25 µm tall and 8 µm wide, T cell about 7 µm, dendritic cell body about 12 µm with processes several times longer, B cell about 8 µm, macrophage about 20 µm; painted cells keep these proportions when shown together, so a T cell beside the airway cell is about a quarter of the cell's height. Virus particles (about 0.1 µm) are shown enlarged inside the airway cell plate and as a separate large plate, each time with a grey tag "virus drawn far larger than real". Clutter rule (owner, 19 Oct): at most about three bright text items at once besides small grey labels; earlier chips dim to grey. Plates are scaled proportionally, never stretched.
